title: Interaction geometry and ground-state properties of sparse quantum lattice models
authors: Alex Gunning, Sebastian Schmid, Zhengxiao Liu, Sridevi Kuriyattil, Aydin Deger, Andrew J. Daley
abstract: We investigate how interaction geometry shapes the low-energy phases of sparse tunable long-range quantum models. We focus on a class of graphs whose degree grows logarithmically with system size, and show how symmetry and frustration in graph connectivity can drive, suppress, and reshape ground-state phase transitions. The central examples are power-of-$p$ graphs, where even and odd values of $p$ exhibit qualitatively distinct behaviour: even-$p$ graphs inherit the rich phase structure of the power-of-two model, while odd-$p$ graphs are governed by geometric frustration. Fibonacci graphs provide a contrasting case, lacking the discrete self-similarity of the power-of-$p$ family but exhibiting a direct geometric mapping between the short- and long-range limits. Across our models, we find that phase structure and criticality are governed by the same effective-geometry principle, unifying our framework for experimentally motivated long-range quantum systems.
summary: This research explores how the geometric arrangement of interactions dictates the low-energy phases of complex quantum lattice models on sparse graphs. By analyzing power-of-$p$ and Fibonacci structures, the authors establish an 'effective-geometry principle' that unifies understanding across different interaction regimes. The findings are crucial for designing and predicting the behavior of experimentally realized long-range quantum systems.
main_problem: The study investigates how the geometric structure of interactions dictates the low-energy quantum phases and phase transitions in sparse, long-range quantum lattice models.
main_result: Phase structure is governed by an 'effective-geometry principle,' showing distinct behaviors for even vs. odd power-of-$p$ graphs, and revealing symmetries (like those in Fibonacci graphs) that map short-range physics onto long-range limits.
method: The analysis employs a combination of analytical techniques (e.g., diagonalization in momentum space), numerical simulations (DMRG, Monte Carlo), and scaling arguments to characterize ground states across various interaction regimes.
model_or_system: The models are sparse quantum lattices, including power-of-$p$ graphs and Fibonacci graphs, analyzed using both Transverse Field Ising Models (spin systems) and fermionic hopping Hamiltonians. Interactions decay with distance $d$ as $J_d \propto d^s$.
key_observables: Ground-state phase diagrams, spectral gaps ($\Delta E$), entanglement scaling (area/volume law), and density-density correlation functions ($g_2(d)$).
important_parameters: The interaction exponent $s$ acts as a primary control knob, determining the relative weight of short vs. long-range interactions; graph structure (e.g., $p=2$ vs. $p=3$) is crucial.
main_assumptions: The analysis often relies on mapping complex systems to effective 1D geometries or assuming specific asymptotic limits ($s 	o -\infty$ or $s 	o +\infty$).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate phase diagrams for different graph types, show spectral gap closing/reopening as a function of the interaction exponent $s$, and compare correlation functions based on system size parity (even vs. odd N).
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares results across multiple graph families (power-of-$p$ vs. Fibonacci) and models (spin vs. fermionic), establishing a unified 'effective-geometry principle' that governs phase transitions regardless of the specific lattice structure.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, general framework for understanding how topology and connectivity dictate quantum many-body physics in systems with long-range interactions, which is highly relevant to engineered quantum materials or artificial lattices.

FIG. 2. Energy gap analysis characterising phases of the classical Ising model on power-of-p and Fibonacci graphs. (a) Power- of-two phase diagram, representative of all even p. Four distinct phases appear in the thermodynamic limit. As p increases, the first critical point (located at s = −2 for p = 2) shifts towards s = −1. (b) Power-of-three phase diagram, representative of all odd p. Three phases occur in the thermodynamic limit. The antiferromagnetic (AFM) configuration remains a ground state for all s; for s > 0, an extensive manifold of competing states becomes degenerate with the AFM. (c) Fibonacci graph for even Fibonacci system sizes Nfib = 34, 144, 610, . . . . No phase...

FIG. 3. Recursive construction of ground-state configurations for power-of-even p graphs. For p = 2 (top), the system size is doubled by appending a globally flipped copy of the previous configuration, yielding an antiferromagnetic ordering of two effective blocks (shown in green/red). Iterating this step gen- erates larger system sizes. For general even p (bottom), the construction proceeds analogously by concatenating p copies of the previous configuration with alternating sign, producing an antiferromagnetic arrangement of p effective blocks.

FIG. 4. Antiferromagnetic state on the p = 3 graph revealing minimal frustration. (Right) The power-of-three graph with each interaction distance d = 3i generating a closed cycle on the ring. Cycles corresponding to d = 1 (black), d = 3 (purple), and d = 9 (peach) are shown. Spins on odd sites are up (blue) and spins on even sites are down (red), corresponding to the antiferromagnetic configuration. (Left) Each colored cycle is unraveled into a one-dimensional chain. Since all cycles have odd length, an antiferromagnetic ordering necessarily frus- trates one bond per cycle, visible at the chain ends. This is the minimal number of frustrated bonds possible on an odd- length cycle.

FIG. 5. Schematics of quantum phase diagrams for the transverse-field Ising model on logarithmically sparse graphs. Panels (a) and (b) show representative power-of-p graphs: p = 2 for the even-p class with N = 8, 16, 32 and p = 3 for the odd-p class with N = 9, 27, 81. Panels (c) and (d) show Fibonacci graphs for even and odd Fibonacci system sizes, respectively, using the accessible sequences N = 8, 34, 144 and N = 13, 21, 55.
